reference.source: WHO Classification of Tumours: Soft Tissue and Bone / standard orthopaedic oncology texts
clinicalPearls: A rare benign cartilage-forming tumour that characteristically arises in the epiphysis or apophysis of a long bone in the skeletally immature
Common sites include the proximal humerus, distal femur and proximal tibia, and it typically presents in the second decade of life
Presents with chronic localised pain, often with an adjacent joint effusion and reduced range of movement
Radiographs show a well-defined lytic epiphyseal lesion, frequently with a thin sclerotic rim and internal matrix calcification
Histology shows chondroblasts with grooved nuclei, scattered osteoclast-type giant cells and a chicken-wire pattern of pericellular calcification
Most lesions harbour a characteristic H3F3B histone gene mutation, a useful diagnostic marker
Treatment is usually curettage with grafting of the cavity, with attention to protecting the adjacent growth plate and joint surface
reference.pathophysiology: Chondroblastoma is a benign neoplasm of immature cartilage-producing cells (chondroblasts) that arises in the secondary ossification centre, explaining its typical epiphyseal or apophyseal location in growing bone. The tumour is composed of sheets of chondroblasts with characteristic nuclear grooves, admixed osteoclast-like giant cells and a distinctive fine pericellular (chicken-wire) calcification of the chondroid matrix. Recurrent driver mutations in the histone gene H3F3B underpin its development and provide a diagnostic immunohistochemical and molecular signature. Although benign, the lesion can breach the growth plate or extend to the articular surface, and rare pulmonary implants have been reported.
additionalDifferentials: Giant cell tumour of bone (usually skeletally mature)
additionalInvestigations: Plain radiographs demonstrating a well-defined lytic epiphyseal lesion with a sclerotic margin
CT to characterise matrix calcification and cortical integrity
MRI to assess marrow oedema, joint involvement and soft-tissue extension
Image-guided or open biopsy with histopathology
Immunohistochemistry and molecular testing for the H3F3B mutation
Chest imaging when atypical or aggressive behaviour raises concern for pulmonary spread
redFlags: Aggressive features or rapid growth suggesting clear cell chondrosarcoma
Articular collapse or secondary joint damage
Extensive growth-plate involvement threatening future limb growth
Pulmonary nodules suggesting the rare benign pulmonary implants
reference.prognosis: With adequate curettage and grafting the prognosis is very good, though local recurrence can occur, particularly with incomplete removal or aggressive lesions. Malignant behaviour is exceptional, and rare pulmonary implants are usually indolent.
pitfalls: Confusing an epiphyseal chondroblastoma in a child with giant cell tumour of bone, which favours mature bone
Overlooking clear cell chondrosarcoma in the differential of an epiphyseal cartilage lesion
Damaging the growth plate or articular surface during curettage
Attributing joint symptoms to primary arthropathy and missing the underlying lesion
references: WHO Classification of Tumours: Soft Tissue and Bone
management: This is a benign, locally aggressive lesion, so local control with preservation of the growth plate and joint surface is the goal, not systemic cancer therapy
Primary treatment is intralesional curettage of the lesion followed by filling the cavity with bone graft or bone cement
Local adjuvants such as high speed burring, cryotherapy, or phenol can be applied to the curetted cavity to reduce recurrence risk
Radiofrequency ablation is a reasonable less invasive alternative for small, favourably located lesions
Surgical planning must protect the adjacent growth plate and articular cartilage given the risk of growth arrest or joint damage in skeletally immature patients
Wide resection is not first line for a benign lesion and is reserved for extensive, destructive, or repeatedly recurrent disease after curettage has failed
Local recurrence is managed with repeat curettage using the same principles and the same attention to growth plate and joint preservation

There is no established role for chemotherapy in ordinary chondroblastoma; systemic therapy is considered only for rare pulmonary implants or atypical aggressive behaviour and should prompt referral rather than empirical treatment
Radiotherapy has no established primary role given the benign nature of the tumour and the added long term risk of radiation near the growth plate in children
Monitor with surveillance imaging, plain radiographs supplemented by MRI as needed, to detect local recurrence, with closer follow up after incomplete excision or in aggressive looking lesions
Follow clinically for joint function and for any growth disturbance related to growth plate involvement or surgical violation of the physis
Consider chest imaging when the lesion behaves aggressively, since rare and usually indolent pulmonary implants have been described
Refer to an orthopaedic oncology multidisciplinary team from diagnosis for biopsy planning, surgical planning around the physis and joint, and molecular confirmation
Refer promptly for atypical features suggesting clear cell chondrosarcoma, for extensive growth plate or articular threat, for recurrence after curettage, or for pulmonary nodules on imaging
